text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Christian Democrat (CDU) general secretary Peter Hintze denies a story in the Le Parisien daily that it the party has received funds from France's Elf-Aquitaine.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel says denounced as improper Iran's refusal to accept the return of its ambassador and said his country would not submit to "blackmail".
- Speaking at mass May Day rallies, leaders of German unions call for unemployment to be tackled, working hours to be cut and for cuts to the tax burden on workers.
- Protesters clash with police in Berlin after May Day demonstrations.
HANDELSBLATT
- Unions call for shorter working hours, while demonstrators clash with police in Berlin on May Day.

- Postbank AG, the banking arm of the Germany's Post AG mail service, puts aside differences and reaches agreement with Post AG on co-operation over the use of post office counter space to distribute its services.
- Total German tax revenues continue to fall with state of Bavaria reporting a fall of 8.8 percent in April compared to last year.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Police break up march by hundreds of neo-Nazis in northern German town of Muenden and detain 150 protesters.
- German Trade Union Federation chief Dieter Schulte calls for reduction to mass unemployment.
- Foreign Minister Kinkel says will not submit to blackmail after Iran refuses to accept the return of the German ambassador.
- CDU denies media report that the party received funds from France's Elf-Aquitaine.
DIE WELT
- German Trade Union Federation repeats calls for a cut in the average working week to 32 hours.
- Foreign Minister Kinkel says will submit to blackmail by Iran.

- Chancellor Helmut Kohl tells the Cologne Stadt Anzeiger daily he thinks the resistance of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in the upper house of parliament to planned tax reforms will not hold out.
